runtimes.name: GenieX
runtimes.description: On-device inference runtime for Qualcomm Snapdragon that pulls, caches, and runs language and vision-language models on the Hexagon NPU, Adreno GPU, or CPU, dispatching either to llama.cpp with Qualcomm's Hexagon backend or to the Qualcomm AI Engine Direct runtime, through a CLI, an OpenAI-compatible local server, and Python, Android, and C SDKs.
runtimes.runtime_boundary: Represents the GenieX software runtime, not the Snapdragon silicon it targets and not Qualcomm AI Hub, the hosted model-compilation and device service from which pre-compiled bundles are fetched. The project was formerly published as NexaAI/nexa-sdk; that repository now redirects to qualcomm/GenieX, and the reviewed product name and owner are GenieX and Qualcomm, described in its own documentation as the community version of Qualcomm GENIE. It is not llama.cpp, which it vendors as a submodule and dispatches to, and not Qualcomm AI Engine Direct, the proprietary Qualcomm runtime reached through a separate plugin repository. Because the product exists to run models on the user's own device and its chat session and local server are how that capability is exercised, it classifies as a runtime rather than an assistant under ADR 015.
runtimes.model_management: geniex pull downloads a model into a local cache from Hugging Face, Qualcomm AI Hub, Docker Hub, or a local directory or AI Hub zip archive, prompting for a GGUF precision where several exist and recording an inferred model type. geniex model list enumerates AI Hub models with a build for the detected chipset, geniex model set-type rewrites the cached manifest to switch between the language-only and multimodal load path, and geniex config get or set chipset controls chipset detection. Gated Hugging Face repositories are reached through GENIEX_HFTOKEN, HF_TOKEN, or the cached Hugging Face token file in that priority order. The local server does not auto-download; a model must be pulled first. No removal command is documented.
runtimes.hardware_requirements: Execution is confined to Qualcomm Snapdragon; the documentation states there is no x86 or non-Snapdragon ARM build. The validated set is Snapdragon X Elite and X2 Elite on Windows ARM64, Snapdragon 8 Elite and 8 Elite Gen 5 on Android, and Dragonwing IQ-9075 and IQ-8275 on Linux ARM64, with chipset auto-detection on all three and an explicit chipset required for Qualcomm AI Hub pulls from the Android SDK. The llama.cpp runtime reaches the Hexagon NPU, the Adreno GPU through OpenCL, and the CPU, with a hybrid per-tensor Hexagon-plus-CPU scheduler and optional spreading across several HTP cores; the Qualcomm AI Engine Direct runtime is NPU-only and coerces other compute-unit requests with a warning. Python must be an ARM64 build.
runtimes.operational_controls: A compute unit is selected per run as npu, gpu, cpu, hybrid, or an explicit HTP device list, and sampler and model flags including context length are set on the same command. Logging has six levels set by flag or the GENIEX_LOG environment variable. Speculative decoding is enabled with a draft model and draft-token bounds, and reports an accepted-draft ratio in the profiling block. The bundled server exposes a Swagger UI at its root and accepts any non-empty API key without checking it. Qualcomm AI Engine Direct bundles have precision, context length, and KV-cache size baked in and reject attempts to change them at runtime.
strengths: Two runtimes behind one interface give both breadth and depth on the same device: any community GGUF from Hugging Face runs on NPU, GPU, or CPU through llama.cpp, while Qualcomm AI Hub bundles run pre-compiled and pinned to the Hexagon NPU.
Model lifecycle is a complete product surface, covering pull from four sources, local cache, precision selection, chipset-aware listing, manifest editing, and gated-repository authentication.

The documentation is unusually specific about limits, naming the validated chipset list, the compute-unit alias mapping, the baked-in constraints of pre-compiled bundles, and the exact error returned when audio is sent to an unsupported runtime.
tradeoffs: Hardware coverage is deliberately confined to Qualcomm Snapdragon, so the runtime cannot serve any other fleet, and the Qualcomm AI Engine Direct path additionally requires a bundle compiled for the specific chipset.
Serving capability is interactive rather than concurrent: no batching, parallel-request handling, KV-cache management, or distributed serving is documented, and the server performs no authentication.
Observability is limited to log levels, a benchmarking tool, and per-run throughput output; there is no metrics or health endpoint for an operator.
The project is published as a developer preview, and the NPU path depends on proprietary Qualcomm runtime libraries rather than being open source end to end.
runtimes.license_note: The repository publishes a BSD-3-Clause license file covering GenieX itself, and its NOTICE file lists bundled Go, C/C++, Python, and Android dependencies under MIT, Apache-2.0, and BSD terms, none of which restrict or alter the project's own license; bindings/python/LICENSE is a symlink to the same root file. The Qualcomm AI Engine Direct execution path, however, is not open source: the geniex-qairt submodule resolves to qualcomm/geniex-qairt-plugin, whose own third-party notices state that the QAIRT headers under qnn-api/ and the prebuilt Windows, Android, and Linux runtime libraries are proprietary Qualcomm Technologies code governed by the Qualcomm AI Runtime SDK end-user licence agreement and explicitly not relicensed under BSD-3-Clause. The README also states that use of the project is subject to Qualcomm's terms of use. An open-source product built around a proprietary accelerator runtime is a mixed_source boundary. The proprietary component is vendored as a git submodule, so its notices live in a separate repository and are recorded as dated web terms rather than a pinned blob in this record's own tree.

license_evidence.scope: Repository-wide license file for the GenieX SDK, CLI, server, and bindings

Qualcomm AI Runtime SDK headers and prebuilt runtime libraries that carry the NPU execution path, vendored through the geniex-qairt-plugin submodule and governed by the Qualcomm AI Runtime SDK end-user licence agreement. The submodule's own third-party notices state these files are not relicensed under BSD-3-Clause. The evidence sits outside this record's repository, so it is recorded as dated web terms rather than a pinned blob.

runtimes.name: llama.cpp
runtimes.description: Dependency-free C/C++ inference implementation for language and vision-language models, consumed as a library, command-line tool, and bundled OpenAI-compatible server across a wide range of hardware backends.
runtimes.runtime_boundary: Represents the llama.cpp project and the tools it ships. Downstream products that embed it, including Ollama, LM Studio, LocalAI, and Jan, are separate boundaries and are not represented by this record.
runtimes.model_management: Models load from local GGUF files or are fetched directly from Hugging Face through a repository flag. The project provides quantization and conversion tooling rather than a managed local model store.
runtimes.hardware_requirements: The project documents a backend matrix spanning CPU vector extensions on x86, ARM, and RISC-V alongside CUDA, HIP, Metal, Vulkan, SYCL, and further vendor backends. CPU and GPU hybrid inference partially accelerates models larger than available accelerator memory.
runtimes.operational_controls: The bundled server exposes configurable parallel slots, continuous batching, multi-GPU split modes, a Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint, and a slot monitoring endpoint, each settable by flag or environment variable.
strengths: Backend coverage is the broadest in the collection, spanning CPU vector extensions, CUDA, HIP, Metal, Vulkan, SYCL, and additional vendor backends.
The bundled server documents continuous batching, configurable parallel slots, multi-GPU split modes, and Prometheus-compatible metrics.
Distributed execution across machines is available through the project's RPC backend.
tradeoffs: Execution is limited to the project's own GGUF format, so weights published in other formats require a conversion step.
There is no managed local model store; model retention, naming, and cleanup are the operator's responsibility.
Capability varies by build configuration, and several documented backends are marked in progress.
runtimes.license_note: The repository publishes a single MIT license file covering the inference implementation and bundled tools.

runtimes.name: LM Studio
runtimes.description: Desktop application and local server for discovering, downloading, and running language models on a personal machine, with a command-line interface and headless mode for unattended hosts.
runtimes.runtime_boundary: Represents the local model runner and its server. Its chat window is how local execution is exercised rather than a broad conversational workspace with durable projects and connected information, so the product is curated as a runtime rather than an assistant.
runtimes.model_management: Models are discovered and downloaded from Hugging Face inside the application and managed through its interface or the lms command-line tool, which also controls the daemon and server.
runtimes.hardware_requirements: Documented requirements cover Apple silicon on macOS 14 or newer, x64 systems with AVX2 and ARM Snapdragon X Elite on Windows, and x64 or ARM64 on Ubuntu 20.04 or newer. Intel-based Macs are not supported and at least 4 GB of dedicated video memory is recommended on Windows.
runtimes.operational_controls: Inference runtimes are selected automatically per model and can be managed and updated from a dedicated runtimes surface. The server can be started and stopped from the application or the command-line tool.
strengths: Ships llama.cpp engine variants for CPU, CUDA, Vulkan, ROCm, and Metal alongside an Apple MLX engine, selecting an engine and offload parameters automatically.
Model discovery, download, and management are integrated into one interface with a command-line equivalent.
Provides a headless mode for servers and continuous-integration hosts in addition to the desktop application.
tradeoffs: The application core is proprietary; only the command-line tool and client SDKs are published under an open license.
Execution is limited to GGUF and MLX weights, and MLX is available only on Apple silicon.
Operational visibility is confined to in-application server logs, with no documented metrics endpoint.
runtimes.license_note: The application and its inference core are governed by proprietary terms that grant a non-transferable license for personal and internal business use. The separately published command-line tool and client SDKs are MIT licensed, which makes the product an open wrapper over a closed operational core.

runtimes.name: LocalAI
runtimes.description: Self-hosted server presenting compatible text, embedding, image, and audio APIs over interchangeable local inference backends, with a model gallery and a web interface.
runtimes.runtime_boundary: Represents the self-hosted gateway and the backends it manages, not the individual inference engines it can load and not any hosted service.
runtimes.model_management: Models are installed from a built-in gallery through the web interface or the command-line tool, and backends are downloaded automatically to match detected hardware.
runtimes.hardware_requirements: Dedicated container images cover CPU-only operation alongside NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Vulkan acceleration. The project documents automatic detection of available GPU capability and states that a GPU is not required.
runtimes.operational_controls: A built-in web interface manages installations and configuration. A distributed mode registers GPU worker nodes with a front-end coordinator for scaling beyond one host.
strengths: Presents OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic Messages, and Open Responses APIs over one self-hosted endpoint, spanning text, embeddings, images, and audio.
A model gallery plus automatic backend selection removes most manual setup for mixed hardware.
Documents container, orchestrated, and distributed multi-node deployment paths.
tradeoffs: Capability depends on which backend serves a given model, so behaviour is not uniform across the catalogue.
As a gateway it inherits the limits of the engines it loads rather than optimising execution itself.
Published operational visibility is centred on the web interface rather than a documented metrics surface.

runtimes.name: MLC LLM
runtimes.description: Machine-learning compiler and deployment engine that converts and compiles language models into platform-native binaries, then executes them on MLCEngine through Python, a command line, a REST server, and Swift, Kotlin, and JavaScript SDKs across desktop GPUs, phones, and the browser.
runtimes.runtime_boundary: Represents the MLC LLM package, its conversion and compilation tooling, and the MLCEngine runtime. It is not Apache TVM, the general-purpose tensor compiler and TensorIR stack it is built on and installs as a separate dependency; TVM supplies the code generation, while this record covers the model definitions, quantization schemes, engine, and serving surfaces layered above it. The browser path is delivered by the sibling mlc-ai/web-llm package, documented here as the web backend of MLCEngine but published and versioned separately. The iOS and Android chat applications built from this repository are demonstrations of the SDKs, not an assistant workspace, so the project stays on the runtime side of the ADR 015 test.
runtimes.model_management: A model reference of the form HF://org/repo resolves against the Hugging Face Hub, downloading pre-quantized weights into a local cache and compiling a model library on first use, after which both are reused. Custom models go through mlc_llm convert_weight to quantize a Hugging Face checkpoint into the project's own sharded parameter format, mlc_llm gen_config to emit mlc-chat-config.json and process tokenizers, and mlc_llm compile to produce the platform binary; the result can be uploaded back to the Hub. Packaging tooling bundles libraries and weights into iOS and Android application builds. There is no pinning, listing, or removal command for cached artifacts.
runtimes.hardware_requirements: The project's platform table documents AMD, NVIDIA, and Intel GPUs on Linux and Windows through Vulkan, with ROCm and CUDA as vendor backends; Apple and Intel GPUs on macOS through Metal; Apple A-series GPUs on iOS and iPadOS through Metal; Adreno and Mali GPUs on Android through OpenCL; and WebGPU with WebAssembly in the browser. The server accepts a device string of cuda, metal, vulkan, rocm, opencl, or auto. There is no documented CPU-only execution path, and compiling for a new target requires the TVM compiler installed alongside the package.
runtimes.operational_controls: The server takes one of three preset engine modes — interactive, local, and server — which set maximum concurrent sequences, total sequence length, and prefill chunk size, each overridable individually along with tensor-parallel shards, GPU memory utilization, prefix-cache recycling, context or sliding-window size, and attention-sink size. Speculative decoding is selected per launch as small-draft, Eagle, or Medusa with an additional draft model. Per-request event logging is enabled with a tracing flag, and CORS origins, methods, headers, and credentials are configurable. There is no authentication, metrics endpoint, or health endpoint.
strengths: One compiler and one engine target an unusually wide set of execution surfaces — desktop GPUs on three operating systems, iOS and Android phones, and WebGPU in the browser — with the same OpenAI-compatible interface on each.

Compilation is a first-class, documented workflow: weight conversion, quantization configuration, model-library compilation, packaging for mobile builds, and defining a new model architecture each have their own reference page.
The server exposes tensor-parallel sharding, prefix caching, configurable batch sizing through engine modes, and three families of speculative decoding without requiring a separate orchestrator.
tradeoffs: Nothing runs without conversion and compilation: weights must be transformed into the project's own quantized shard format and paired with a compiled model library for the exact target, so a stock checkpoint cannot be pointed at and served directly.
Operational visibility is minimal, with per-request tracing and a CLI statistics command but no metrics endpoint, health endpoint, authentication, container image, or orchestration guidance.

The supported model architecture list is narrower than mainstream server engines, and the published documentation is still versioned 0.1.0 with pages of differing freshness, so capability must be confirmed per model and per release.
Browser execution is documented here but shipped from a separate repository and package, so the reviewed runtime's own release does not carry that surface.
runtimes.license_note: The repository publishes a single verbatim Apache-2.0 license file covering the compiler, engine, and tooling. The accompanying NOTICE file carries only the project name and a contributor copyright line and imposes no additional terms. The Apache TVM dependency is installed separately and is not vendored into this repository.

Usable as a Python module, a set of command-line tools, and a local server without additional components.

The bundled server is explicitly documented as not recommended for production because it implements only basic security checks.

runtimes.name: Ollama
runtimes.description: Local model runner that packages model download, storage, and serving behind one CLI, desktop application, and REST API on the user's own hardware.
runtimes.runtime_boundary: Represents the self-operated Ollama runtime. Ollama Cloud, the hosted tier operated by the same organization, is a separate managed inference service record. The model library Ollama distributes is not part of this record.
runtimes.model_management: Models are pulled, pushed, created from a Modelfile, copied, listed, and deleted through the CLI and REST API. Safetensors weights and adapters can be imported into the local store.
runtimes.hardware_requirements: Documented NVIDIA support requires compute capability 5.0 or newer with driver 550 or newer; AMD support runs through ROCm; Apple silicon runs through Metal. runtimes.operational_controls: Server environment variables govern loaded-model count, parallel requests per model, and queue depth. CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES restricts GPU selection. Running models and versions are inspectable through the API.

Documents OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible endpoints alongside its native API, plus embeddings, tool calling, structured outputs, and vision.
Installers, container images, and hardware support are documented per platform with explicit driver and compute-capability floors.
tradeoffs: Concurrency is limited to parallel request slots and multiple loaded models; the documentation describes no continuous batching or distributed serving.
Documented accelerator coverage spans NVIDIA, AMD, and Apple silicon; Vulkan and Intel paths are not part of the published hardware support matrix.
Operational visibility is limited to running-model and version endpoints with no documented metrics endpoint.

runtimes.name: ONNX Runtime GenAI
runtimes.description: Cross-platform generative inference library that implements the token generation loop for ONNX models, including pre- and post-processing, KV-cache management, sampling, constrained decoding, and adapters, consumed through Python, C, C++, C#, and Java APIs.
runtimes.runtime_boundary: Represents the generate() API layer published as onnxruntime-genai, not ONNX Runtime itself, which is the general-purpose ONNX inference engine and execution-provider framework underneath it. Products that embed this library, including Foundry Local, Windows ML, and the Visual Studio Code AI Toolkit, are separate boundaries. The library has no server, no network endpoint, and no graphical interface; it is exercised through host application code, which places it on the runtime side of the ADR 015 runtime-versus-assistant test as an embedded library rather than an assistant.
runtimes.model_management: Models are ONNX directories containing a genai_config.json alongside graph and tokenizer assets, loaded from a local path; a model-package layout can bundle several hardware variants of one model and select at load time. The repository ships a model builder that converts and quantizes Hugging Face PyTorch, quantized PyTorch, and GGUF sources into the required ONNX layout, and the project documents downloading prebuilt ONNX models through the Hugging Face CLI or Foundry Local. There is no runtime model store, registry, or removal command; LoRA adapters use a documented .onnx_adapter flatbuffers file and multi-adapter switching.
runtimes.hardware_requirements: The project's support matrix documents Linux, Windows, macOS, and Android on x86, x64, and arm64, with CPU, CUDA, DirectML, NvTensorRtRtx, OpenVINO, QNN, and WebGPU acceleration; AMD GPU support is listed as roadmap. Qualcomm Snapdragon NPU execution requires the separate onnxruntime-qnn execution-provider plugin and a model packaged with compiled QNN graph artifacts, and Python, C, C++, and C# are supported while Java requires a source build.
runtimes.operational_controls: Search, sampling, and KV-cache behaviour are configured through genai_config.json and per-generator search options; provider options such as the Qualcomm HTP performance mode are set on the model configuration. Runtime options can terminate and restart a generation session and toggle ONNX Runtime profiling per token during generation.
strengths: One generation loop targets CPU, CUDA, DirectML, and Qualcomm NPU hardware across Windows, Linux, macOS, and Android from Python, C, C++, C#, and Java bindings.
Constrained decoding through LLGuidance provides Lark grammar, JSON schema, and regex outputs for tool calling, alongside multi-LoRA adapters with a published adapter file specification.
The repository documents a paged-attention engine with continuous batching, and both draft-model and n-gram speculative decoding, with explicit statements of their limits.
tradeoffs: Execution is limited to ONNX graphs, so any other weight format must first be converted with the model builder or Olive, and per-execution-provider artifacts such as QNN context binaries are built separately.
There is no server, endpoint, authentication, metrics, or health surface; only in-process profiling and logging, so operational visibility depends entirely on the host application.

The continuous-batching Engine API is documented as a transitional host-facing surface that is not thread-safe, and the published support matrix still lists speculative decoding as roadmap while the repository documents it as implemented, so capability varies by version and build.
runtimes.license_note: The repository publishes a single MIT license file covering the generate() API implementation. A ThirdPartyNotices.txt file lists the licenses of bundled dependencies and does not restrict or alter the project's own MIT terms.

runtimes.name: OpenVINO Model Server
runtimes.description: C++ inference server that serves generative and classic deep-learning models compiled by OpenVINO onto Intel CPU, GPU, and NPU targets, exposing OpenAI-compatible, KServe, and TensorFlow Serving endpoints over REST and gRPC.
runtimes.runtime_boundary: Represents the model server, not the OpenVINO toolkit it is built on: the toolkit supplies the runtime plugins, model conversion, and optimization tooling and is a separate boundary, as are the OpenVINO GenAI library and the models published in Intel's Hugging Face collections. The server is headless and operated as a container, a binary package, a Windows service, or an in-process C API host; it ships no graphical or conversational interface, which keeps it on the runtime side of the ADR 015 runtime-versus-assistant test.
runtimes.model_management: Models live in a versioned model repository on local storage, S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob, or the Hugging Face Hub. A pull mode downloads models in OpenVINO IR or GGUF form without starting the service, and a conversion path exports and quantizes PyTorch sources through optimum-cli. Version policies choose which numbered versions are served, configuration changes and new or removed models are applied at runtime without restarting, and a model cache speeds repeated loads.
runtimes.hardware_requirements: Execution targets Intel hardware: x86 CPUs including Xeon, Intel integrated and discrete GPUs through the OpenVINO GPU plugin built on oneDNN and OpenCL, and NPU devices, on Linux and Windows as containers or binary packages. GPU and NPU use requires host drivers and, for containers, the accelerator-enabled image and device passthrough. NPU execution uses the stateful pipeline and static shapes only, so dynamic models must be reset with a fixed batch size or shape, while CPU and GPU use the continuous-batching pipeline.
runtimes.operational_controls: The server takes device selection per model through target_device, including HETERO and AUTO virtual devices with latency, throughput, and cumulative-throughput hints. LLM graphs configure KV-cache size, maximum active sequences, dynamic split fuse, prefix caching, and cache eviction. Generative endpoints can require a bearer API key from a file or environment variable, and request limits cover execution streams, gRPC threads, REST workers, message size, and memory quota.
strengths: One server presents OpenAI-compatible chat, completions, responses, embeddings, image generation, and audio endpoints, a Cohere-compatible rerank API, and KServe and TensorFlow Serving APIs over both REST and gRPC.

Generative serving uses continuous batching and paged attention with prefix caching, cache eviction, dynamic split fuse, and draft-model speculative decoding, and classic models run through a DAG scheduler and MediaPipe graphs.

Operations are mature: Prometheus-compatible metrics with a documented metric list, versioned model repositories on cloud storage, runtime configuration reload, Docker, bare-metal, Windows service, Kubernetes and OpenShift deployment, and a C API for in-process embedding.
tradeoffs: Hardware coverage is Intel-only; there is no documented CUDA, ROCm, or Metal execution path, so the server does not serve mixed-vendor accelerator fleets.
Generative models are normally served from OpenVINO IR exported with optimum-cli, GGUF support is limited to text generation on a published model list, and NPU serving requires static shapes.

The documentation states that gRPC and REST endpoints provide no access restrictions or traffic encryption by default, with an API key available only for the generative /v3 endpoints, so production exposure depends on a reverse proxy; scaling beyond one host is by replicas rather than multi-host model parallelism.
runtimes.license_note: The repository publishes a single Apache-2.0 license file covering the server, reproduced unchanged in the release package directory. A thirdparty-licenses directory carries the licenses of the components redistributed in the binary and container packages and does not restrict the server's own terms.

runtimes.name: TensorRT LLM
runtimes.description: NVIDIA inference and serving engine for language, multimodal, and visual generation models, combining custom GPU kernels, a PyTorch-native runtime, and an optional ahead-of-time compiled TensorRT engine path behind one Python LLM API and an OpenAI-compatible server.
runtimes.runtime_boundary: Represents the TensorRT LLM library and its trtllm-serve, trtllm-bench, and trtllm-eval tools, operated on GPUs the user controls. It is not TensorRT, the general-purpose NVIDIA deep-learning inference library and engine-builder it can compile through, and it is not NVIDIA's managed offerings, which hold their own serving contract and belong to the inference-service collection. NVIDIA Dynamo and Triton Inference Server orchestrate this engine and are separate boundaries, as is NVIDIA Model Optimizer, the offline quantization toolkit whose checkpoints this runtime loads.
runtimes.model_management: Models are named by Hugging Face repository identifier or local checkpoint directory at engine construction, with a pluggable checkpoint-loading architecture that separates config loader, weight loader, and weight mapper so a new checkpoint format can be added without changing the engine. Pre-quantized checkpoints produced by NVIDIA Model Optimizer load directly; offline quantization is a separate step in that project. Multiple LoRA adapters are supported per request. There is no runtime model store, pinning, or removal command, and the legacy TensorRT backend additionally requires an engine build step whose artifact is specific to the GPU architecture and parallelism configuration it was built for.
runtimes.hardware_requirements: The published support matrix limits the reviewed runtime to Linux on x86_64 or aarch64 with NVIDIA GPUs from the Ampere, Ada Lovelace, Hopper, Grace Hopper, and Blackwell architectures including GB200 NVL72; architectures outside that list are community-supported only. Available precisions vary by architecture, with FP8 documented from Ada Lovelace onward and INT4 AWQ or GPTQ with FP8 activations requiring compute capability 8.9 or higher. Windows and macOS are not supported, and a Jetson path exists only on a separate release branch.
runtimes.operational_controls: Parallelism is configured at launch through tensor, pipeline, expert, context, and data-parallel sizes, alongside KV-cache dtype and block reuse, chunked prefill, CUDA graph batch sizes, scheduler policy, and speculative decoding mode. trtllm-serve exposes /health, /metrics, and /version, with the metrics endpoint reporting runtime iteration statistics including GPU memory use and in-flight batching detail. Anonymous telemetry is collected by default and can be disabled by environment variable, a marker file, a Python config field, or a CLI flag. A stated deprecation policy gives a three-month migration window with runtime warnings.
strengths: Serving capability is unusually complete, covering in-flight batching, paged KV cache with block reuse, chunked prefill, an overlap scheduler, prefill-decode disaggregation, and tensor, pipeline, expert, context, and data parallelism across single-node and multi-node deployments.

Quantization coverage is broad and documented per model, spanning NVFP4, MXFP4, several FP8 recipes, FP8 and NVFP4 KV cache, and W4A8 or W4A16 AWQ and GPTQ, with a published model-by-model support table.

The server implements OpenAI Chat, Completions, and Responses endpoints plus a dedicated embeddings subcommand with dynamic batching, alongside guided decoding, multi-LoRA serving, and multimodal input.
tradeoffs: Execution is confined to NVIDIA GPUs on Linux; there is no CPU, AMD, Apple, or Windows execution path in the reviewed support matrix, so the runtime cannot serve a mixed fleet.

The project carries two backends whose model coverage differs, and the current PyTorch backend is primary while the TensorRT engine-building path is documented separately, so a capability confirmed for one backend is not evidence for the other.

Several headline features are labelled beta or prototype in the documentation, including disaggregated serving and AutoDeploy, and the published support matrix page is stamped almost a year older than the installation guide, so version-specific verification is required.

The repository ships a visual-generation model directory under a restricted community license with revenue-based commercial terms, so redistribution and commercial use of the whole tree are not uniformly Apache-2.0.
runtimes.license_note: The root LICENSE file states Apache-2.0 as the project license and then reproduces three further license texts covering code derived into the project from other open-source projects. Portions derived from CUTLASS, causal-conv1d, and flash-attention are BSD-3-Clause; portions derived from Bitcoin Core, flash-linear-attention, InstructEval, and MiniMax Sparse Attention are MIT; portions derived from FlashInfer, Mamba, Quack, SGLang, Text Generation Inference, Transformers, XGrammar, vLLM, and Baseten's suffix-automaton speculative decoding are Apache-2.0. The same file also reproduces the LTX-2 Community License Agreement, which the file scopes explicitly to tensorrt_llm/_torch/visual_gen/models/ltx2/ and which is not an open-source license: it requires entities with annual revenues of at least ten million dollars to obtain a separate paid commercial license, imposes use-based restrictions, and requires derivatives to be distributed under the same agreement. That directory exists in the repository and carries its own NOTICE pointing back to the root file. The Apache-2.0 core is therefore accompanied by a restricted component, which is why this record is classified open_core rather than mixed_open_source; GitHub reports NOASSERTION because the file opens with a custom header and concatenates four license texts.

runtimes.name: vLLM
runtimes.description: High-throughput inference and serving engine built around paged attention, continuous batching, and multi-dimensional parallelism for operator-controlled accelerators.
runtimes.runtime_boundary: Represents the self-hosted serving engine. Managed services that deploy vLLM on a customer's behalf are separate inference-service boundaries, and the models it serves are not part of this record.
runtimes.model_management: Models load from Hugging Face repositories or local paths at server start, with adapter and quantization support. Weights are pinned by the launch configuration rather than managed through a runtime model store.
runtimes.hardware_requirements: Documented execution covers NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and x86, ARM, and PowerPC CPUs, with further accelerators available through a plugin architecture that includes TPU, Gaudi, Spyre, and Ascend targets.
runtimes.operational_controls: Parallelism strategy, batching, prefix caching, and speculative decoding are configured at launch. The project documents an observability surface for a running server alongside distributed deployment guidance.
strengths: Serving capability is the most complete in the collection, covering continuous batching, chunked prefill, prefix caching, and tensor, pipeline, data, expert, and context parallelism.
Quantization and weight-format coverage spans FP8, MXFP8, NVFP4, INT8, INT4, GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF, and compressed-tensors.
Serves an OpenAI-compatible API alongside an Anthropic Messages API and gRPC, with structured outputs and tool calling.
tradeoffs: The engine targets accelerator-backed server deployment; it is not packaged as a desktop application and has no graphical interface.
Accelerators beyond NVIDIA and AMD depend on plugins whose maturity varies by target.
Model selection is fixed by launch configuration, so changing weights means restarting or running another instance.
runtimes.license_note: The repository publishes a single Apache-2.0 license file covering the serving engine.

runtimes.name: Xinference
runtimes.description: Self-hosted supervisor-and-worker server that launches language, embedding, reranking, image, audio, and multimodal models on interchangeable inference backends and presents them through one OpenAI-compatible API, a web interface, a command line, and a Python client.
runtimes.runtime_boundary: Represents the self-hosted community edition and the backends it launches, not the engines themselves: vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp through xllamacpp, MLX, and Transformers each keep their own boundary, and vLLM has its own record. It is distinct from LocalAI, the other reviewed compatibility gateway, which ships its own Go server with bundled C++ backends and a gallery aimed at a single mixed-hardware host, whereas Xinference is a Python cluster of a supervisor and workers that places model replicas across machines. Xinference Enterprise and the maintainer's hosted plans hold the serving contract for their customers and are outside this record. The bundled web interface is a management and test console for locally launched models, not a conversational workspace, so the record stays on the runtime side of the ADR 015 runtime-versus-assistant test. The separately licensed enterprise edition and the maintainer's hosted plans are outside this record.
runtimes.model_management: A built-in catalogue launches models by name with one command, downloading from Hugging Face or ModelScope and caching files locally for later starts. Custom models are registered from a local path or a JSON specification, cached files are listed and removed through the command line and web interface, running models are terminated to free resources, and LoRA modules are attached at launch from operator-supplied paths. Per-model virtual environments isolate backend dependencies, and the backend is selected automatically from model format, quantization, and hardware unless the operator names one.
runtimes.hardware_requirements: Installation is documented on Linux, Windows, and macOS with backend extras installed per model type. CUDA devices are required for the vLLM and SGLang backends, the MLX backend targets Apple silicon, llama.cpp covers CPU and GPU hosts with automatic GPU-layer estimation, and Ascend NPU execution is documented through torch-npu with the Transformers backend only, which the project states is slow on some chips and steers to its enterprise MindIE engine. Multi-GPU and multi-node execution is available for the engines that support it.
runtimes.operational_controls: Models launch with a chosen engine, replica count, GPU count, and optional per-replica placement onto named workers. A database-backed authentication system with users, permissions, API keys, and optional OIDC single sign-on is enabled by default and can be disabled by environment variable. Supervisor and worker Prometheus metrics exporters, cluster start and stop commands, and a web interface complete the operator surface.
strengths: One OpenAI-compatible endpoint covers chat, completions, embeddings, reranking, image, audio, and multimodal models launched from a large built-in catalogue with a single command.
Cluster operation is first class: a supervisor with registered workers, replica placement, distributed inference across machines on vLLM, SGLang, and MLX, and shared KV cache between vLLM replicas.

Operational controls are unusually complete for a gateway, with database-backed authentication and API keys enabled by default, OIDC single sign-on, supervisor and worker metrics exporters, and per-model virtual environments.
tradeoffs: Execution quality, batching, and quantization coverage come from the selected backend, so behaviour is not uniform across the catalogue and each backend carries its own installation constraints.
Ascend NPU support in the open-source edition runs only on the Transformers backend, and the project directs users needing the MindIE engine to a separately licensed enterprise edition.
The Python dependency surface is heavy and version-sensitive, with vLLM and SGLang documented as conflicting inside one environment and several backends requiring separate installation commands.
runtimes.license_note: The repository publishes a single Apache-2.0 license file covering the self-hosted edition, which is what this record represents. The maintainer also markets a separately licensed enterprise edition and hosted plans, and its own Ascend installation guide names the MindIE engine as unavailable outside that edition. Those commercial terms are published only as a placeholder page at the time of review, so the enterprise edition is noted as an adjacent product boundary rather than recorded as a reviewed license.
